turns.response_html:
Your intuition is spot on. You have essentially reverse-engineered the entire process purely through mechanical logic. Paper-mâché (French for "chewed paper") relies exactly on the combination of a structural skeleton, a fibrous skin, and a binding adhesive.

To take your theory into practice, there are just a few subtle mechanical adjustments to optimize the strength and finish of the build.

The Three Components

1. The Armature (The Skeleton)

As suspected, paper-mâché has no structural integrity on its own while wet. An internal support—called an armature—is vital.

  • Materials: Cardboard ribs provide excellent rigid planes, crumpled aluminum foil or newspaper creates lightweight volume, and wire allows for bendable limbs or curves.
  • Preparation: Tight joints are critical. Everything should be wrapped securely in masking tape before any wet paper touches it. The paper will mirror the texture underneath, so a smooth armature yields a smoother final surface.

2. The Paste (The Binder)

Soaking the paper in plain water would just break down the wood fibers without locking them back together. The liquid must be an adhesive matrix. Two classic formulas work best:

  • The PVA Method (Stronger & Mold-Resistant): Mix 2 parts white school glue or wood glue with 1 part warm water. This creates a durable, slightly flexible plastic matrix when dry.
  • The Flour Method (Traditional & Cheap): Mix 1 part flour with 1 part water until it reaches a smooth, heavy-cream consistency. Adding a pinch of salt helps prevent mold growth during the drying phase.

3. The Paper (The Skin)

Standard newspaper, newsprint, or brown packing paper is ideal because its long, loose fibers absorb paste beautifully.

  • The Trick: Tear the paper into strips instead of cutting it. Cut edges leave sharp, distinct ridges that create weak points and a rough texture. Torn edges have exposed, frayed fibers that blend into one another seamlessly, creating a smooth, monolithic shell.

The Execution Workflow

Pro Tip: Once 3 to 4 total layers have dried completely, the shell becomes remarkably rigid. It can then be sanded down with fine-grit sandpaper, coated with a primer (like gesso), and painted or sealed just like wood or plastic.
